issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-related trigger content is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Ambulances is coherent for medical trauma, but military topics suggests a very different trauma context and is therefore clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge/get-even rumination implies an identifiable perpetrator or assailant. That does not fit a child's life-threatening illness trauma, which is not typically organized around interpersonal assault. This creates a cross-node/content mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies is not a clearly coherent trigger for trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness unless the illness was specifically neonatal/perinatal, which is not indicated. In this profile it sits awkwardly alongside the more plausible medical trigger of ambulances.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Physical self-harm used to stop thinking about the event is possible in PTSD, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile: the only triggers are situational reminders, with no corroborating threat, appraisal, or memory items suggesting the kind of overwhelming internal distress usually linked to this strategy. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

vignette: Ravi is a 50-year-old South Asian male who has been experiencing significant distress following his daughter's life-threatening illness. Ravi and his wife had brought their young daughter to the hospital after she developed severe respiratory issues that required intensive care. The experience was harrowing, marked by long nights in sterile corridors waiting for updates from doctors and watching his child hooked up to monitors and machines. Since then, Ravi has found himself repeatedly triggered by certain stimuli that remind him of those days in the hospital. Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place evokes intense anxiety, as he is reminded of the sleepless nights spent worrying about his daughter's health. He now prefers sleeping with his wife beside him for comfort and reassurance, even though this creates some tension in their relationship due to differing schedules. Medical procedures also trigger Ravi's distress. Any time he has a medical examination or needs to visit a doctor, the antiseptic smell of hospitals overwhelms him, flooding him with memories of his daughter lying motionless under bright lights and surrounded by equipment. This has led him to avoid routine check-ups and even minor treatments for fear of re-experiencing that traumatic environment. Ravi has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with these triggers and the overall anxiety he feels. He often ruminates about how to get even with those who might have been responsible, particularly hospital staff or perceived negligent individuals. This rumination is fueled by his belief that somehow someone could have prevented his daughter's illness from becoming so severe. He also mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios to feel prepared for any potential recurrence of her condition, which only adds to his stress and makes it difficult to focus on his work as an animator. Ravi frequently seeks reassurance from his wife and colleagues about whether he is doing enough to protect his family or if something terrible might happen again. This constant need for validation has strained his relationships, particularly with his wife who feels that Ravi's hypervigilance makes it hard for her to provide the support he needs. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have taken a toll on Ravi's daily life and work as an animator. His focus at the studio has waned due to constant worrying and rumination, leading to missed deadlines and critical feedback from his supervisors. He feels isolated and overwhelmed by the persistent fear that something terrible might happen again. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a series of minor but significant incidents where he became acutely aware that his anxiety was affecting not just him but also those around him. His wife had expressed her concern about their relationship, and colleagues at work were beginning to notice his decline in performance. Ravi is most afraid of losing control again and being unable to protect his family from another crisis. He hopes therapy will help him regain a sense of stability and security so he can return to living a fulfilling life with his loved ones.
